combination_brief: GSAT-30: Launched 17 Jan 2020 on Ariane-5 VA-251; about 3,357 kg at 83 E with 12 C-band and 12 Ku-band transponders. Ku covers India; the C-band has extended coverage over the Gulf, many Asian countries and Australia. Replaces INSAT-4A; used for VSAT, TV uplink, DTH, DSNG and telecom. | GSAT-31: Launched 6 Feb 2019 on Ariane-5; about 2,535 kg at 48 E with 40 Ku-band transponders over India and its islands. Used for VSAT, DTH, cellular backhaul, ATMs, stock-exchange networks and e-governance. | GSAT-24: Launched 22 Jun 2022 on Ariane-5; about 4,180 kg at 83 E with 24 Ku transponders. First NSIL demand-driven satellite, with all capacity leased for DTH television. | GSAT-11: Launched 5 Dec 2018 on Ariane-5; about 5,854 kg at 74 E. Ku and Ka multi-beam payload (about 32 user beams plus hub beams) with more than 16 Gbps throughput for broadband, rural and island connectivity. | GSAT-29: Launched 14 Nov 2018 on GSLV Mk III-D2; about 3,423 kg. Ka and Ku multi-beam payload, with an optical-communication experiment and a high-resolution camera. Connectivity for remote areas such as Jammu and Kashmir and the North-East. | GSAT-N2 (GSAT-20): Launched 19 Nov 2024 on Falcon 9; about 4,700 kg. Ka-band high-throughput payload with 32 beams (8 narrow over the North-East, 24 wide across India) and about 48 Gbps, for broadband, in-flight and maritime connectivity under NSIL. | CMS-01 (GSAT-12R): Launched 17 Dec 2020 on PSLV-C50; about 1,410 kg. Extended C-band services over the Indian mainland, Andaman and Nicobar and Lakshadweep islands; replaces GSAT-12. | GSAT-7 (Rukmini): Launched 30 Aug 2013 on Ariane-5; about 2,650 kg at 74 E. UHF, S, C and Ku payloads giving the Indian Navy secure communications over a footprint of about 2,000 nautical miles across the Indian Ocean Region. | GSAT-7A (Angrika): Launched 19 Dec 2018 on GSLV-F11; about 2,250 kg. Ku-band communication for the Indian Air Force, linking ground radar stations, airbases and airborne early-warning aircraft, also supporting Army aviation. | CMS-03 (GSAT-7R): Launched 2 Nov 2025 on LVM3-M5; about 4,410 kg, the heaviest satellite launched from Indian soil. Multi-band payloads giving the Navy secure communications across a wide Indian Ocean footprint. ISRO reports that corrective measures drawn from the NVS-02 anomaly were tested on this satellite. | Together: Ku and C-band satellites carry TV, VSAT and telecom traffic; Ka-band high-throughput satellites (GSAT-11, GSAT-29, GSAT-N2) add broadband capacity; naval and air-force satellites add secure links. Overlapping slots between 48 E and 93.5 E give redundancy, load sharing and backup if one satellite is lost. Global scope is Partial because this covers only the Indian Ocean sector.

combination_members: Cartosat-3 + Cartosat-2 series (2D, 2E, 2F, 2A) + Resourcesat-2 / 2A + HySIS + Oceansat-3 (EOS-06)
combination_brief: Cartosat-3: Third-generation Cartosat launched 27 Nov 2019 on PSLV-C47 into a sun-synchronous orbit at about 509 km. Panchromatic imaging at about 0.25 to 0.28 m (ISRO's finest) plus multispectral bands, over a swath of roughly 16 km, with agile pointing for off-nadir, stereo and rapid re-targeting. Best for city-scale mapping, infrastructure, change detection and defence. Limits: narrow swath, daylight and clear sky only, tasked rather than systematic. | Cartosat-2 series (2D, 2E, 2F, 2A): Cartosat-2D (Feb 2017), 2E (Jun 2017) and 2F (Jan 2018) are agile SSO satellites at about 500 km with about 0.65 m panchromatic imaging and a swath near 10 km; Cartosat-2A (2008, about 1 m class) is listed operational but ageing. Several satellites tasked together raise the revisit over a target. Best for cartography, utilities, urban growth and cadastral work. Limits: cloud and darkness, narrow swath. | Resourcesat-2 / 2A: Resourcesat-2 (2011) and Resourcesat-2A (Dec 2016, the one listed operational) fly at about 817 km in SSO with three cameras: LISS-4 (5.8 m, steerable), LISS-3 (23.5 m, includes shortwave infrared) and AWiFS (56 m, about 740 km swath, about 5-day repeat). Best for crop acreage, forest cover, water bodies and land use. Limits: moderate resolution, cloud cover. | HySIS: Hyperspectral Imaging Satellite launched 29 Nov 2018 on PSLV-C43, SSO about 636 km. Records about 55 contiguous bands across visible-near-infrared and shortwave infrared at about 30 m, which allows identification of minerals, crop stress, vegetation type and coastal conditions. Limits: modest resolution and swath, limited tasking, large data volumes. | Oceansat-3 (EOS-06): Launched 26 Nov 2022 on PSLV-C54, SSO about 720 km. Carries OCM-3 (13-band ocean colour with a very wide swath of over 1,000 km), SSTM (thermal sea-surface temperature), SCAT-3 (Ku-band scatterometer for ocean-surface wind) and ARGOS (data collection). Gives about 2-day coverage. Best for chlorophyll, algal blooms, fishery advisories, cyclone winds and sea-surface temperature. Limits: coarse over land. | Together: The SSO fleet above plus EOS-08, whose infrared imager adds night-time and thermal views (fires, heat, volcanoes) over the tropics. EOS-08 cannot support Polar or Global requests.

rationale: ISRO has no MEO imaging satellite. Use SSO (resolution), LEO, or GEO (cadence).
alternative_if_not_available: Switch orbit to GEO: INSAT-3DS/3DR/3D (coarse full-disk, Indian Ocean sector only)
combination_brief: Not available in MEO. Nearest ISRO combination (GEO): INSAT-3D family (3DS, 3DR, 3D): INSAT-3D (Jul 2013), INSAT-3DR (Sep 2016, 74 E) and INSAT-3DS (Feb 2024, GSLV-F14) are ISRO's geostationary weather satellites at about 74 E to 82 E. Each has a 6-channel Imager (visible and shortwave infrared at about 1 km, mid and thermal infrared at about 4 km, water vapour at about 8 km); 3D and 3DR also carry a 19-channel Sounder for temperature and humidity profiles, plus data-relay and search-and-rescue payloads. Full disk about every 30 minutes with faster sector scans. Limits: cannot see the poles, coarse resolution. | Together: INSAT imagers give coarse views every 15 to 30 minutes and EOS-05 adds finer multispectral and hyperspectral detail once operational. Use GEO to detect fast-changing events such as cyclones, floods and fires, then task SSO satellites for high-resolution follow-up.

combination_brief: Not available in MEO. Nearest ISRO combination (GEO): EOS-05 (GISAT-1A): 2,367 kg, I-2K bus. isro_satellites: NISAR, RISAT-1A (global); RISAT-2B family (about +/-45 deg latitude only)
rationale: Only NISAR/RISAT-1A provide beyond-tropics coverage.
combination_brief: NISAR: NASA-ISRO radar observatory of about 2,400 kg launched 30 Jul 2025 on GSLV-F16, operational since 7 Nov 2025. Orbit about 747 km, 98.4 degrees, 6 am / 6 pm crossing. NASA supplies the L-band SAR (24 cm) and a 12 m mesh reflector; ISRO supplies the S-band SAR (10 cm), the satellite bus and the launch. SweepSAR gives a 242 km swath at 3 to 10 m with an exact 12-day repeat, in single, dual and quad polarisation; data are free and open. Best for biomass, soil moisture, ground deformation, glaciers, sea ice, floods and crops. Limits: systematic rather than on demand, no daily revisit. | RISAT-1A (EOS-04): Launched 14 Feb 2022 on PSLV-C52; about 1,700 kg, SSO about 529 km. C-band SAR with several modes from a few metres to about 50 m resolution and a wide swath in coarse mode; about 25-day repeat. Best for crops, soil moisture, flood mapping and forestry. Limits: coarser than X-band, slow repeat. Its sister RISAT-1B (EOS-09) was lost in the May 2025 PSLV-C61 failure. | RISAT-2B / 2BR1 / EOS-01: RISAT-2B (May 2019), RISAT-2BR1 (Dec 2019) and EOS-01 / RISAT-2BR2 (Nov 2020, status to verify) carry X-band SAR on a 3.6 m radial-rib antenna in LEO inclined about 37 degrees at roughly 550 to 580 km. Spotlight, strip and wider modes reach sub-metre to a few metres. The inclined orbit gives repeated passes over India and the tropics, so this is the fastest-revisit SAR family, but it does not reach polar latitudes. Best for defence, borders, ship detection, floods and disaster response. | Together: The X-band RISAT-2B family provides fast, high-resolution tasked views of India (minimum revisit about daily), while NISAR adds systematic wide-area L and S-band coverage. For Polar and Global requests only the SSO members (NISAR, RISAT-1A) apply.

NASA supplies the L-band SAR (24 cm) and a 12 m mesh reflector; ISRO supplies the S-band SAR (10 cm), the satellite bus and the launch. SweepSAR gives a 242 km swath at 3 to 10 m with an exact 12-day repeat, in single, dual and quad polarisation; data are free and open. Best for biomass, soil moisture, ground deformation, glaciers, sea ice, floods and crops. Limits: systematic rather than on demand, no daily revisit. | RISAT-1A (EOS-04): Launched 14 Feb 2022 on PSLV-C52; about 1,700 kg, SSO about 529 km. C-band SAR with several modes from a few metres to about 50 m resolution and a wide swath in coarse mode; about 25-day repeat. Best for crops, soil moisture, flood mapping and forestry. Limits: coarser than X-band, slow repeat. Its sister RISAT-1B (EOS-09) was lost in the May 2025 PSLV-C61 failure. | Together: NISAR gives systematic L-band and S-band maps (forest biomass, soil moisture, deformation, ice) and RISAT-1A adds C-band. The different wavelengths respond to different surface properties, so combining them improves classification of vegetation, flooding and ground movement.

combination_brief: Not available in LEO. Nearest ISRO combination (GEO): NavIC (IRNSS-1B, 1I, NVS-01): India's regional navigation system: a base layer of 3 GEO and 4 IGSO satellites broadcasting L5 (1176.45 MHz) and S-band signals, with an open Standard Positioning Service and an encrypted Restricted Service. Primary area India plus about 1,500 km; extended area about 30 S to 50 N and 30 E to 130 E. Second-generation NVS satellites add an L1 signal for interoperability with GPS and Galileo and indigenous rubidium clocks. Status Oct 2026: IRNSS-1B, IRNSS-1I and NVS-01 fully operational for positioning; five older satellites messaging only; NVS-02 stranded; NVS-03 awaiting launch. | Together: NavIC GEO and IGSO satellites supply position and time over India and the surrounding region; GAGAN adds corrections and integrity data for aviation; the partly working older satellites still carry messaging and disaster alerts. Capability is reduced until NVS-03 and later satellites are launched.
